Folks, let me pour a cold glass of reality onto this entire anti-Flash situation. Outside of IT folks and geeks, no one honestly cares. It's sad, but true.
People did start to care, finally, after all those years.
I have FlashBlock installed. Use on demand only.

I'm not sure how you could say end users don't care. They might not know its name, but they surely suffer from a crappy plugin that is slow, insecure, frequently crashing and always nagging for updates. What you don't know can definitely hurt you.

I've had two people recently ask me why Youtube keeps acting up, being slow, not showing them videos, taking up so much memory, etc. etc. etc. and I have advised each of them to follow instructions to remove Flash and set Youtube to use HTML5. So far, at least 3 or 4 months later, zero complaints about anything, and in fact, one of them hit me up a couple of days ago and thanked me for "fixing my Youtube".

The end users notice problems, they just don't know what to point a finger at.

I always try to think of these things like cars because I know nothing about cars. I can recognize issues like weird noises or wonky steering, but I have no clue what's wrong. Lots of people use computers out of necessity like I use a car, but they have the same clueless nature about how they work.

I wish everyone knew more about how computers worked so it'd be easier to talk to them in these situations, but some people just want a working computer, and that's pretty easy to get these days. So a diminishing percent of computer users are computer savvy because they don't have to be and computers are only getting more complicated and diverse over time. I don't know if this needs to be fixed, or if it can be, but I thought it was worth mentioning.

A lot of people would care if they'd know about the problems, but they don't read any tech news. Most normal users don't know that HTML5 is a thing and that Flash is obsolete and even a potential threat to their security.
The Internet still uses it, so I keep my computer set up for Flash.

Which means you will continue to #1 be vulnerable to all the issues that come with one of the worst pieces of software ever, and #2 slow down the rate that flash is ditched.

What sites do you use currently that use flash?

Whenever possible, my deployments simply no longer include Flash in base images nor is it part of the configuration and setup after the initial build.

If someone somehow does need Flash in their organization for their work flow (for who knows what flippin' reason in this day and age) I install it on an individual as needed basis. Same goes for Java, and any other browser plug-in.

So as IT-Folk, I'm doing my part to spread the Flash retirement gospel :)

TLDR Rant section:

  • Flash & Java helped with the creation of "update prompt hypochondria"
  • Flash & Java have shit the bed security-wise a suspicious amount of times in the past 10-15 years
  • Adobe & Oracle are oblivious to update packaging that doesn't piss users and deployment technologists off
  • I think both plugins have wasted an unfathomable amount of man-hours during their life spans
  • apt-get, yum, pacman, and friends > All windows based deployment mechanisms - including those that attempt to poorly mimic our Linux utilities

Start of flash rant

I find older users who had admin rights on their workstations who worked on Windows workstations during the pre-UAC era still have a latent fear of clicking yes to any program which asks them seemly at random if it should update from fear they'd unleash malware hell on their systems. Flash helped spawn the culture of unsolicited auto update hypochondria which still to this day some of my users still suffer from.

Honestly with the amount of times Flash, Java, and the like have pissed me off with auto update prompts at inappropriate times while supporting various organizations, I can't blame these users.

I hate the bloody programs for additional reasons that have nothing to do with their insensible, retarded amount of security flaws. Adobe & Oracle, even though are massive companies somehow manage to shit the bed all-the-flippin-time when it comes to their update packaging. I feel they assume every single network environment has the required resources to pull off the miraculous weekly or even daily silent auto update process that also shuts their silly user update prompts off. And it's not difficult to pull off for seasoned deployment techs that have the time and resources to keep up with that, but that doesn't make it any easier for IT support firms helping many small-medium clients or the designated 'computer guy' in the smaller organizations.

So even though it's a required evil because of the blatant almost seemly will-full security bed shitting, the upkeep for Flash, Java, and similar IMHO are massive wastes of man hours.

End of flash rant.

The general public doesn't care about most tech-related topics beyond "does this allow/prevent me from doing X?", even then in many cases it's a hard sell unless it affects them personally.

Still, in many cases, if we convince IT staff with decision power, then the rest have no choice but follow. They probably won't even notice change happening. They just want to do X.

This is why corporations dump money and tools at universities, and why FOSS enthusiasts should be proactive.

Hello fine kinksters!

There have been a couple of posts and PM's asking what exactly is the plan for this community, so I'm going to lay out my thinking, and hear what you all have to say. Obviously this is still a very small community, so anything is up for change in the future (assuming voat takes off and doesn't die a firey server crash death - but that's beyond my control).

I've been an active member of the bdsmcommunity over on reddit for years now, and I think it's an excellent resource, and one of the better bdsm discussion forums on the web. With that in mind we have a blank slate here, and that gives us an opportunity to improve upon any flaws that might exist.

Personally, I would like to see the concept of "Your kink is not my kink, and that's ok" practiced here. If you've been a member of the BDSM community for any length of time you've probably heard disparaging comments made towards it, or even yourself. I think it's very important we don't fall victim of that sort of groupthink ourselves, and ostracize people who are perhaps on the edge of the "bdsm" sphere, or who engage in activites that are a hard no for you. The big example and sticking point for me would be people who engage in risk(ier) behavior then others - self bondage, needleplay, etc. Occasionally there have been posts made to reddit regarding these topics, where the upvoted comments include stuff like "gross", or heated accusations of gross negligence. To be specific, I'm referring to posts about completely consensual behavior

Comments like that don't create a good discussion, and they certainly don't change the mind of the person that posted. Posts like that, I think, mainly serve to make the poster feel morally superior. I won't stand for that, because I don't stand for people saying the same thing about my kinks, to make themselves feel better. As long as we expect and push for people outside our community to not ridicule us, or treat us like freaks because of what we do in our own bedrooms, we don't get to do the same to others. I don't think a discussion about any bdsm topic should be off limits, and I don't think those discussions should focus on making someone feel bad about their sexuality, or kinks.

That being said, I'm not at all talking about non-consensual behavior. Specifically, actual rape, bestiality and pedophilia are not bdsm related, not legal, and not open for any discussion. I don't want someone misunderstanding my meaning there.

The other thing I intend to do differently, is make the rules very clear, and enforce them openly. Unfortunately voat doesn't have a wiki yet. Once it does I intend to make a thorough explanation of what posts are allowed and what posts are not, and I would also like to make moderator decisions as open as possible, including listing why people are banned, should I ever have to use the ban hammer. Secrecy and uneven application of rules breeds resentment and distrust in an online community, and I intend to avoid that.

For something voat specific, I've turned on a requirement where to be able to downvoat, you need to have at least one CCP (aka someone needs to have upvoated at least one comment or post you've made here). This has the effect of preventing anyone from wandering in and downvoating everything they see, and also means our posts don't get posted to /v/all, which I think is a positive. Agreed?

Finally, please let my know what you think of the CSS.

Any and all suggestions are welcome!

I always use the cheap 1sqft patio squares to discourage any digging. I run a row of them around the outside of the yard fence. I have also used them inside of a kennel to stop digging. They basically make a cheap, movable concrete floor.

We don't have a dog but do have predators in the area (coyotes, fisher cat, etc). When building our coop/run I dug down approx 4-6 inches and extended the hardware cloth underground to discourage digging. If digging is problematic you could take hardware cloth and attach it to the coop run and right angle it to lay on the ground for a foot or so around the coop and cover it with a little soil.
